region.en: Pasig, Rizal province, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省帕西格（敘述者居地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5a 'How Suan became Rich', eBook #8299

summary.en: Poor Suan borrows a building post from his rich friend Pedro, whose envy drives him to accuse Suan before the king. On the road Suan accidentally drowns a bather and tears off a carabao's tail, gathering three accusers. The king's literal decisions — post for rice-and-fish, bath for the bather's son, carabao until its tail regrows — are all exploited by Suan, who collects payments from every frightened accuser and finally, razor in hand at Pedro's house, extorts all of Pedro's riches.
summary.zh: 窮漢蘇安向富友佩德羅借屋柱；佩德羅眼紅，竟控告於王前。途中蘇安失手溺死沐浴老人、拉斷水牛尾，招致三路原告。國王照字面判決：柱換飯、以浴償溺、牛尾長全才還牛——蘇安遂逐個向怕事的原告索錢，最後持剃刀上門『取回飯魚』，佩德羅驚恐之下獻出全部家財。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Pasig narrator; archival record. Part of the 'Wonderful Decisions' cycle; Fansler derives it from the Jataka 'Gamani-canda' No. 257.

passages.text: Pedro inherited a great fortune from his parents, but his friend Suan was as poor as the poorest of beggars. Suan borrowed one building post to construct a house that surpassed Pedro's own, and the envious Pedro demanded it back though its removal would destroy the house; refusing to be paid or replaced, he threatened to accuse Suan before the king. On the Monday journey Pedro carried silver, Suan only cooked rice and fish, which he generously shared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'How Suan became Rich'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the broken bridge Suan fell from his jump onto an old man bathing in the river, knocking him silly so that he drowned; Isidro, the son, joined the party to accuse him. Then Suan, helping Barbekin rescue a carabao from the mire, pulled so hard that the tail broke off short, and Barbekin resolved to accuse him too. At the palace the king gave literal decisions: Suan must return the post and Pedro give him his rice and fish; Suan must bathe in the river and Isidro may jump on him; Barbekin must give Suan the carabao until its tail grows to full length.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'How Suan became Rich'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Suan then milked every judgment: Barbekin paid ninety pesos to be quit of the carabao; Isidro, afraid to jump from the high bridge and unable to swim, bought pardon for five hundred pesos; and Pedro, facing Suan's razor as he announced he had come for his 'rice and fish,' cried out that he need not return the post and then, cut at the abdomen's edge, offered all his riches. Thus Suan became the richest man in town by using his tact and knowledge in outwitting his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'How Suan became Rich'; not verbatim.

title.en: The King's Decisions: Juan and the Smell of Money
title.zh: 國王的判決：胡安與金錢之香

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5b 'The King's Decisions', eBook #8299

summary.en: Starving Juan's hunger is satisfied by the fragrance of a rich man's cooking, and the rich man demands payment — for a smell. On the road Juan breaks a horse's tail and frightens a pregnant woman into miscarriage, adding two accusers. The king rules that the smell of food be paid with the smell of silver coins, that the horse-tail regrow before return, and that the wife bear another child before restitution — literal justice that leaves every accuser empty-handed.
summary.zh: 飢餓的胡安被富戶飯香所飽，富人竟索香氣之錢。途中胡安拉斷馬尾、驚致孕婦流產，又添二告。國王判曰：飯香者以銀幣之香償之；馬尾長全方可還馬；妻再生一子方可抵命——照字面執行的判決，令所有原告空手而歸。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Batangas narrator; archival record. Second variant of the 'Wonderful Decisions' cycle derived from Jataka No. 257.

passages.text: Poor Juan, weakened with hunger and fatigue, passed a rich man's house where food was cooking, and the fragrance satisfied his hunger. When the rich man learned that the smell of his food had satisfied Juan, he demanded money; Juan refused, having none, and having neither tasted nor touched the food. They set out for the king's palace to have the matter settled, and on the way gathered more accusers: Juan, helping a man free his horse from a mud-hole, pulled the animal's tail off; and at midnight, lodging downstairs, his sudden frightened shriek so startled the pregnant wife above that she miscarried, and her husband joined the party.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'The King's Decisions'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before the king, the rich man Pedro demanded pay for the smell of his food. The king commanded a servant to fetch two silver coins and place them on the table: 'Now, Pedro, come here and smell the coins. As Juan became satisfied with the smell of your food, so now satisfy yourself with the smell of the money.' Pedro could not say a word. The next decisions followed the same logic: Manuel must give his horse to Juan until another tail grows, and the married man must let Juan have his wife until she gives birth to another child. All three went home discontented — Pedro without pay, Manuel without his horse, and the other without his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'The King's Decisions'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Blind Brothers and the Pagui Tail

region.en: Misamis, Mindanao, Philippines (origin of the narrator's tale)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨米薩米斯（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Pampangan-retold Mindanao tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6a 'The Four Blind Brothers', eBook #8299

summary.en: Sent away to seek their fortunes, four blind brothers feel for cocoanuts in a grove and climb, one after another, a tree whose top had been broken — each fall counted as a 'Bung!' of dropped fruit by the brothers below, until the last one finds his three brothers dead. Weeping, he disturbs the patianac, who give him food, shelter, and the tail of a pagui (sting-ray) to find his fortune. Joined by a lame man, the two frighten a two-headed giant from his own house by dropping the sting-ray tail as a 'hair' — the prediction comes true and they live in the giant's house happily ever after.
summary.zh: 四盲兄弟外出謀生，在椰林中依次攀爬已被颱風折頂的椰樹，逐一墜亡；樹下者只當『咚』的一聲是椰子落地，數到第四聲才知真相。末弟哭聲驚動帕蒂亞納克幽靈，他們憐之，賜食、賜宿，並贈魟魚尾一枚以助其轉運。盲者與跛者同行，將魟尾當作『頭髮』拋下，嚇退雙頭巨人，奪其宅邸——預言應驗，二人從此安居樂業。

sensitivity.note: Tale collected by Fansler from a Pampangan narrator who heard it from a Misamis (Mindanao) boy; archival record. The patianac are Philippine night spirits; the sting-ray tail is a traditional demon-charm.

passages.text: There was once a man who had eight sons, four of them blind, and unable to keep them he sent all away to seek their fortunes. The blind brothers groped along the road, each holding the hand of the other, until in the evening they came to a cocoanut-grove. The eldest took off his camisa china and climbed a tree to gather a bunch of cocoanuts — but the tree broke, and down came the poor fellow. 'One!' cried the youngest brother. 'Three more!' shouted the rest, and 'Don't come down until you have dropped four!' they all cried at once. Who would answer them? Their brother lay dead on the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Four Blind Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: While they waited for the second 'Bung!' the second brother climbed the same tree, and what had happened to the first happened to him, and so to the third in turn. When the youngest heard the third fall, he crept about to find the cocoanuts, and discovered instead that his three brothers lay dead on the ground. He went away crying very loud — and his crying disturbed the patianac, who were trying to sleep. Moved by the poor helpless blind man, they gave him food and shelter for the night, and the tail of a pagui which would help him find his fortune; at daybreak they showed him the way out of the grove.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Four Blind Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The blind man was hailed by a lame man resting under a shady tree, who asked to be carried on his shoulders; so they traveled together to a big, lonely house. When its owner, a two-headed giant, returned, he was afraid to enter but called in a voice of thunder, 'Who's there?' — 'We are big men... so big that the foundation of the house shakes when we walk.' 'Give me a proof!' cried the giant, and the two dropped from the window the tail of the pagui as 'one of our hairs.' The giant looked at it in wonder, convinced that they were more powerful than he, and picking up the 'hair' went away, afraid to face such antagonists in single combat. So the prediction of the patianac came true: the house and all the property of the giant fell into the hands of the blind man and the lame man, and they lived there happily all the rest of their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Four Blind Brothers'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan the Blind Man and the Outlaws' House

region.en: Virac, Catanduanes, Philippines (where the story is common)
region.zh: 菲律賓卡坦端內斯維拉克（故事流行之地）

texts.period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6b 'Juan the Blind Man', eBook #8299

summary.en: Eight blind friends who gather nightly in a cocoanut-grove lose seven of their number to broken typhoon-stumps, counting the falls as dropped fruit. The last, Juan, meets the lame Justo and they travel together, collecting a horn, a rusted axe, a rope, and an old drum. Hiding in a robbers' house, Juan answers the outlaws' challenge with the axe as his 'tooth,' the rope as his 'hair,' the horn as his whistle, and the drum as his stomach — terrifying them into flight. When the quarrel over the money comes, Justo's blow opens Juan's blind eyes and Juan's kick cures Justo's lameness; they divide the money fairly and live as close friends.
summary.zh: 八名盲友夜聚椰林，颱風折頂之樹令七人墜亡，盲者僅聞墜聲誤作椰子。倖存的胡安遇跛者胡斯托同行，沿途拾得號角、鏽斧、麻繩與舊鼓。二人躲進強盜之家，以斧為『牙』、繩為『髮』、號角為哨、鼓聲為肚——嚇得強盜跳窗而逃。分贓起爭執時，胡斯托一掌打開胡安的盲眼，胡安一腳踢癒胡斯托的跛腿；二人平分財富，結為莫逆。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a Virac, Catanduanes narrator; archival record. Fansler traces this tale-family to southern India (Frere's 'The Blind Man, the Deaf Man, and the Donkey').

passages.text: Many years ago there lived near a thick forest eight blind men who were close friends; at night they would go secretly to a neighboring cocoanut-grove, drinking tuba and eating young cocoanuts. One evening a severe typhoon struck the village and broke most of the cocoanut-trees off at the top. The next afternoon the joyous party went to steal fruit, and seven of them climbed the stump-trees while Juan, the youngest, remained below to count the cocoanuts his friends threw down. He had repeated his verse three times when he heard a fall — 'One' — then another and three in close succession: 'Good! five in all. Three more, friends.' A few minutes later he heard two more falls: 'Six, seven — well, only seven... One more for me, friends.' But it was his friends who had fallen, for the trees were only stumps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan the Blind Man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Juan found one of the dead bodies he ran away as fast as he could, until he struck Justo, a lame man, who advised him not to return lest the relatives of the others accuse him of murder. They agreed to travel together — 'Blind man, strong legs; Lame man, good eyes... But we'll walk on two, and we'll see with two' — gathering as they went a horn, a rusted axe, a piece of rope, and an old drum. Then Justo saw a very big house whose door stood open, its walls hung with bolos, spears, and shields; they hid in the ceiling, and when outlaws returned with bloody bolos and a big sack of money, the terrified Justo could not help crying out, 'Ay, here?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan the Blind Man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Ho, you mosquitoes! what are you doing there?' asked the chief of the outlaws. 'Aha, you rascals! we are going to eat you all,' answered the blind man in the loudest voice he could muster. 'To show you what kind of animals we are, here is one of my teeth' — and Juan threw down the rusted axe. 'Look at one of my hairs!' — and he threw down the rope. 'Now listen, you ants, to my whistle!' — and he blew the horn. 'And to show you how big our stomachs are, hear us beat them!' — and he beat the drum. The outlaws were so frightened that they ran away, some even jumping out of the windows. Dividing the money, Justo tried to cheat Juan; in the quarrel Justo struck him in the eyes with the palm of his hand, and the blind man's eyes were opened; Juan kicked Justo so hard that he rolled against a post and his lameness was cured. Seeing that each had done the other a great service, they divided the money fairly and lived ever after together as close friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan the Blind Man'; not verbatim.

title.en: Teofilo the Hunchback and the Giant

region.en: Bicol region, southeastern Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home region)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋東南比科爾地區（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6c 'Teofilo the Hunchback, and the Giant', eBook #8299

summary.en: The wandering hunchback Teofilo, one-eyed and crooked, gathers a rope, a gun, and a duck, and sleeps in what turns out to be a giant's house. Challenged through the wall — 'If you are really a strong man and braver than I, let me see your hair!' — he throws out the rope; for his louse, the duck; for his voice, the gunshot the giant takes for spitting burning coals. The giant flees forever, and Teofilo lives happily in his house.
summary.zh: 流浪的獨眼駝背者特奧菲洛拾得麻繩、獵槍與鴨子，夜宿巨人宅中。巨人隔牆喝令『讓我看看你的頭髮！』——他拋出麻繩；『讓我看看你的蝨子！』——他拋出鴨子；『讓我聽聽你的聲音！』——他開槍，巨人誤以為他吐出的是燒紅的煤，倉皇而逃，永不復返。特奧菲洛從此安居其宅。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a student narrator; archival record. Token-deception variant of the blind-brothers tale-family.

passages.text: Once there lived a hunchback whose name was Teofilo. He was an orphan who got his food by wandering through the woods, sometimes sleeping under large trees; his one blind eye and crooked body would make almost any one pity his miserable condition. One day, wandering for something to eat, he found a piece of large rope, then a gun left against a fence, then caught a duck at a brook — sure of a good meal. Night coming on, he found a house with all its windows open, knocked, and entering, prepared his bed and slept, not knowing he was in a giant's house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Teofilo the Hunchback'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At midnight Teofilo was awakened by a loud voice. Through a hole in the wall he saw a very tall man, taller even than the house itself. 'I smell some one here,' said the giant, trying the locked door. 'If you are really a strong man and braver than I, let me see your hair!' — Teofilo threw out the piece of rope, and the giant was surprised at its size. 'Let me see your louse!' — and Teofilo threw out the duck, and the giant was terrified, for he had never seen such a large louse. 'Well, you seem to be larger than I. Let me hear your voice!' — Teofilo fired his gun, and when the giant heard it and saw it spitting fire, he trembled, thinking the man's saliva was burning coals. Afraid to challenge his strange guest any more, the giant ran away and disappeared forever — and so Teofilo the hunchback lived happily all the rest of his days in the giant's house without being troubled by any one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Teofilo the Hunchback'; not verbatim.

region.en: Albay, Bicol region, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿爾拜省（比科爾，敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6d 'Juan and the Buringcantada', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lazy Juan, gored between two fighting carabaos while trying to help, recovers and travels with his mother, collecting an axe, a rope, and a large drum. In the mansion of the Buringcantada — a one-eyed giant with tusks — mother and son hide in the ceiling; challenged to show a hair, a tooth, and the sound of his stomach, Juan produces the rope, the axe, and the drum. The terrified giant and his guests flee forever, and Juan and his mother live in the house like a rich family.
summary.zh: 懶惰的胡安為救被鬥牛所傷的水牛，反被雙牛角傷背；痊癒後與母親遠行，沿途拾得斧、繩與大鼓。他們藏身於獨眼長牙巨人布林坎塔達的府邸天花板中；應巨人之令展示『頭髮』（麻繩）、『牙齒』（斧頭）與『肚腹之聲』（鼓聲），巨人與賓客嚇得落荒而逃。母子從此在豪宅中過著富人般的生活。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a narrator who heard it from his grandmother; archival record. Token-deception variant; the Buringcantada is a Bicol one-eyed tusked giant.

passages.text: A long time ago, when the Bicols had not yet been welded into one tribe, a couple in the mountains of Albay had one son, Juan, whose father died before the boy was five. Growing up lazy, Juan was dearly loved and indulged by his mother, who told him to help anybody he met that needed help. One afternoon he saw two carabaos fighting and, mindful of her words, went between the animals to help the wounded one — and the two gored him in the back. Recovered, he persuaded his mother to go with him to look for money, gathering on the way an axe, a long rope stretching across the road, and a large drum on a river bank.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan and the Buringcantada'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After about a week's travel they came upon a big house, well decorated with flowers and leaves, with a large hole in the dining-room ceiling. Juan proposed hiding there until they found out who the owner was, and mother and son went up into the ceiling with the axe, the rope, and the drum. Before many minutes the Buringcantada, a giant with one eye in the middle of his forehead and two long tusks projecting from the sides of his mouth, came in with his friends and servants to dine. Juan said in a loud voice that the viands were the best for them — and the giant thundered, 'If you are a big man like me, let me see one of your hairs!' Juan showed the rope; 'Let me see one of your teeth!' — Juan showed the axe; 'Beat your stomach, and let me hear the sound of it!' — and when Juan beat the drum, the Buringcantada and all the guests and servants ran away in fright, never having heard such a sound before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan and the Buringcantada'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Juan and his mother came down from the ceiling. In this house they lived like a rich family, for they found much money in one of the rooms; as for the Buringcantada, he never came back to his house after he left it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan and the Buringcantada'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Manglalabas: The Ghost Who Guarded a Treasure

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋巴盧巴德（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6e 'The Manglalabas', eBook #8299

summary.en: A haunted house in Balubad is emptied by the manglalabas, a spirit that throws stones, pinches the widow, and scatters the furniture. The blind Bulag and hunchback Cuba take shelter in its ceiling with a hatchet and an old gun they found on the road; the ghost's challenge is answered with a gunshot and the hatchet-head as a 'tooth.' The spirit, convinced it faces a powerful being, confesses it haunts the house nightly only to see its buried treasure dug up; the gold is found, the quarrel over division cures both men of their deformities, and they own the house together.
summary.zh: 巴盧巴德一鬧鬼之宅屢遭曼格拉巴斯作祟，家人棄宅而逃。盲者布拉格與駝背古巴借宿閣樓，以路拾的短斧與舊槍應對鬼魂：一聲槍響、一枚『牙齒』（斧頭）令幽靈信服——它坦白夜夜現身只為盼人掘出其藏金。二人掘得金銀，分贓爭執中布拉格眼睛復明、古巴駝背拉直，從此同住大宅。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a narrator who heard it from his father; archival record. The manglalabas is a house-haunting spirit; spirit-possession tag marks the living-with-ghosts situation, interpretively.

passages.text: In the small town of Balubad stood a big house inhabited by a rich family; when the head of the family died, the house grew gloomy and dark. Three days after the death the family began to be troubled at night by a manglalabas, who threw stones at the house, broke the water-jars, moved the beds, pinched the widow while she slept, and emptied all the jars. A band of brave men assembled to fight the spirit, but when they saw that it was a ghost they fled away, and from that time on nobody was willing to pass a night in that house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Manglalabas'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a certain barrio of Balubad lived two queer men — Bulag the blind and Cuba the hunchback — who agreed to go begging together, the blind man carrying the hunchback on his shoulder. On the way Cuba picked up a hatchet and an old gun, and in town they begged until they came to the large abandoned house, where they hid in the ceiling for the night. At midnight the manglalabas came again, shouting that he believed there were new persons in his house; Cuba, frightened, fired the gun, and the ghost, thinking the noise was someone crying, said, 'If you are truly a big man, give me some proofs.' Cuba took the handle out of the hatchet and threw the head down, which the spirit took for one of the teeth of his visitor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Manglalabas'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Convinced that the intruder was a powerful person, the manglalabas said, 'I have a buried treasure near the barn. I wish you to dig it up. The reason I come here every night is on account of this treasure. If you will only dig it up, I will not come here any more.' The next night the two dug near the barn and found many gold and silver pieces. When Cuba kept three-fourths of the treasure for himself, Bulag felt the piles and discovered the cheating; angry, Cuba struck Bulag in the eyes, and they were opened; Bulag kicked Cuba in the back, and his deformity disappeared. They became friends again, divided the money equally, and owned the big house between them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Manglalabas'; not verbatim.

title.en: Sagacious Marcela and the Impossible Tasks

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pampangan oral tale, set before the Spanish era; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7a 'Sagacious Marcela', eBook #8299

summary.en: The king tests Marcela, his clever servant's daughter, with impossible tasks: make twelve dishes of one bird (she sends back a pin — twelve spoons from it first); sell a sheep for six reales and return it alive (she sells only the wool); fetch bull's milk for his physician's prescription. To the last she answers by washing birth-stained bedding at the river the king has forbidden to all others — 'my father gave birth to a child last night' — and the king, conceding that a bull's milk is as absurd, gives her his son in marriage.
summary.zh: 國王連出難題考驗僕人之女瑪塞拉：一鳥做十二道菜——她回敬一枚別針『先做出十二把湯匙』；六里亞爾賣羊且羊須生還——她只賣羊毛；為御醫取公牛之奶——她故意在王獨佔浴河之日洗滌產婦血污衣物，稱『家父昨夜生產』。國王啞口無言，認可公牛產奶同樣荒謬，遂以王子妻之。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from a Licup narrator; archival record. The Clever Lass cycle; Fansler notes a Bicol variant ('Marcela outwits the King') and two Tagalog corrido versions (Cay Calabasa, Rodolfo).

passages.text: Long before the Spaniards came there lived a man, a servant of the king, whose daughter Marcela was beautiful, virtuous, and above all clever. From childhood she had manifested a keen wit and undaunted spirit, refusing even to obey unjust orders from the king, and no question was too hard for her to answer. One day the king conceived a plan to test her: he had his servants carry a tiny bird to her house and tell her to make twelve dishes out of that one bird. After thinking five minutes, Marcela took one of her pins: 'If the king can make twelve spoons out of this pin, I can also make twelve dishes out of that bird.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'Sagacious Marcela'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next the king sent a sheep with orders to sell it for six reales and bring back the money with the very same sheep alive. Marcela cut off the wool, sold it for six reales, and sent the money back with the live sheep. Then the king ordered her to get him a cup of bull's milk for his physician's prescription, or her father would lose his place in the palace — and issued an order that no one was to bathe or wash anything in the river, for he was going to take a bath the next morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'Sagacious Marcela'; not verbatim.

passages.text: That night Marcela and her father killed a pig and smeared its blood over the sleeping-mat, blanket, and pillows; in the morning she took the stained bed-clothing to the source of the river where the king was bathing. In a voice of thunder he demanded why she washed her stuff in the river when nobody but he was to use it that day. 'It is the custom, my lord, in our country, to wash the mat, pillows, and other things stained with blood, immediately after a person has given birth to a child. As my father gave birth to a child last night, custom forces me to disobey your order.' — 'Nonsense! The idea of a man giving birth to a child! Absurd! Ridiculous!' — 'My lord, it would be just as absurd to think of getting milk from a bull.' Then the king, recollecting his order, said, 'Marcela, as you are so witty, clever, and virtuous, I will give you my son for your husband.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'Sagacious Marcela'; not verbatim.

title.en: King Tasio and the Squash in the Jar

region.en: La Laguna province, Luzon, Philippines (where the story is popular)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省（故事流行之地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7b 'King Tasio', eBook #8299

summary.en: Boasting kitchen-servant Juan is set impossible tasks by King Tasio: catch the rolling waves (a rope of seashore sand first), make fifty foods from one bird (stove, pan, and knife of this needle first). Expelled from the palace grounds, Juan rides in on a paragos loaded with earth from his own orchard; commanded to put a big squash into a narrow-necked jar unbroken, he grows a small squash inside the jar on its vine until it fills it — and the king faints before his court.
summary.zh: 自誇的御廚胡安被塔西奧王連出難題：先以海沙搓繩方可捕浪；先以縫衣針造灶、鍋、刀方可一鳥做五十道菜。被逐出宮後，胡安駕著載有自家果園泥土的耙子入宮——『我沒踩您的地』。最後國王令他把大南瓜完封放入小頸瓶；胡安讓幼瓜在瓶中藤上生長，數週後瓜漲滿瓶。國王當著滿朝賓客昏倒在地。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Faustino narrator; archival record. Clever-servant cycle, companion to Sagacious Marcela.

passages.text: Juan was a servant in the palace of King Tasio, and one day was heard in the kitchen saying he knew more than anybody else in the palace. The king called him and told him to go down to the seashore and catch the rolling waves: 'You said that you are the wisest man in the palace. Go and catch the waves of the sea for me.' 'That's very easy, O king! if you will only provide me with a rope made of sand taken from the seashore.' The king, not knowing what to answer, next commanded him to make fifty kinds of food out of a small bird — 'if you will only provide me with a stove, a pan, and a knife made out of this needle.' Again the king did not know what to do, and angrily expelled Juan: 'Don't you let me see you walking on my ground around this palace without my consent!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'King Tasio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day King Tasio saw Juan in front of the palace, riding on his paragos drawn by a carabao. 'Did I not tell you not to stand or walk on my ground around this palace? Do you mean to mock me?' — 'Will your Majesty's eyes please see whether I am standing on your ground or not? This is my ground,' and he pointed to the earth he had on his paragos, taken from his own orchard. Furious, the king handed Juan a squash and a jar whose neck was small: 'Put this squash into this jar. See that you do not break either the squash or the jar.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'King Tasio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Juan went home and put a very small squash, growing in his garden, inside the jar — but did not cut it from the vine. After a few weeks the squash had grown big enough to fill the jar; he then picked off the squash enclosed in the jar and presented it to the king before all the servants, courtiers, and visitors. As soon as the king saw the jar with the squash in it, he fainted, and it was many hours before he recovered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'King Tasio'; not verbatim.
